PA Bill Would Ban Online Gambling Bonuses, VIP Perks

Published October 31, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

A group of Pennsylvania state representatives has introduced a bill that would rewrite much of how online sportsbooks and internet casinos operate in the state, banning sign-up bonuses, bonus bets, and VIP loyalty programs outright and capping how much and how often customers can deposit. House Bill 2879, titled the Online Gambling Public Health and Consumer Protection Act, was filed by Rep. Tarik Khan (D-Philadelphia) along with eight other Democrats and one Republican, and has been referred to the House Gaming Oversight Committee.

What the bill would change

The bill's deposit rules would apply across both online sportsbooks and iGaming platforms: no more than two deposits per 24-hour period, no funding via credit cards or government assistance cards, no gambling gift cards, and a $5,000 cap on total deposits over any 180-day span unless an operator completes a formal affordability check. Players between 21 and 25 would face additional limits, including a $2 maximum wager per play on online casino games and a mandatory 30-day cooling-off period triggered by losing $750 in a day or $2,500 in a month. Every bettor, regardless of age, would have to set daily and monthly loss limits before placing a first wager, and could lower that limit immediately but only raise it after a cooling-off period.

On the marketing side, the bill targets some of the industry's most common promotional tools directly: it would eliminate microbets and proposition bets from sports betting, ban push notifications soliciting bets or deposits, prohibit sign-up bonuses, bonus bets, and VIP programs, bar marketing language like "risk-free," and block all gambling advertising between 8 a.m. and 10 p.m. and during live sports broadcasts.

The reasoning, and the pushback

In a memo to colleagues, Khan and his cosponsors wrote that "problem gambling is increasingly recognized as a public health issue because of the significant harm it can cause to mental health, financial security, and family stability," adding that aggressive marketing by operators has deepened concerns about debt and well-being, particularly among young adults. Unnamed opponents cited in coverage of the bill argue the restrictions would hand a competitive advantage to unregulated offshore gambling sites that operate outside U.S. jurisdiction and face none of these rules, while licensed operators maintain that responsible-gaming commitments are already central to their businesses.

Why it matters for Pennsylvania bettors and casino players

HB 2879 is newly introduced and faces a real time constraint: Pennsylvania's 2026 legislative session ends November 30, and any bill that hasn't passed by then doesn't carry over into 2027. That makes swift committee action unlikely to translate into a quick vote this year, but the bill still signals where a meaningful bloc of lawmakers wants Pennsylvania's rules to head — toward tighter deposit and loss limits and away from the bonus-driven marketing that's defined the legal online casino and sportsbook market since launch. Players in Pennsylvania don't face any of these restrictions yet, since the bill hasn't cleared committee, let alone passed, but the proposal is worth watching for anyone following how states are starting to regulate promotional offers and spending limits more directly.
